To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the extent of cytidine methylation in the Escherichia genome is determined at single-base resolution, 2) cytidine methlylation is partially removed from the genome during growth phase and 3) cytidine methylated DNA is involved in regulation of stationary phase gene expresion.
DNA cytosine methylations in E. coli are partially unmethylated in exponentially growing bacteria and that these partially methylations are associated with the risk of cytosine to thymine conversion.
DNA cytosine (C) methylation in Esche- richia coli is highly correlated with the risk for spontaneous, non- synonymous C to T mutation and regulates stationary phase gene expression.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the epigenetic regulation of bacterial gene expression and genome stability by cytosine methyaltion and its role in bacterial stress response.
the role of cytosine methylated DNA in bacteria and its impact on genome architecture and gene regulation.
the role of DNA cytosines methylation in bacteria.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the DNA methylation system in bacteria is a mechanism to regulate gene expression in response to environmental changes.
cytosine methlyation in E. coli regulates stationary phase gene expression.
DNA cytosine methyltransferases in E. coli are involved in the regulation of gene expression in stationary phase.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
DNA cytosine methylations in E. coli have a regulatory role in gene expression during the transition to stationary phase.
DNA cytosine methyltransferase (Dcm) plays a role in the regulation of stationary phase gene transcription by controlling the expression of the stationary phase sigma factor (rpoS).
cytosine methyaltion regulates gene expression in stationary phase cells.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the extent of cytidine methylation in E. coli varies depending on the growth phase.
cytosine methlylation is a widespread phenomenon in bacteria, with a large number of methylated sites that are only partially methylatied in growing cells.
cytosine methyation can have a regulatory role in bacteria, as it has in mammals.
